verses.1:
Al-Mizan states that the chapter warns and gives glad tidings through accounts of Moses, David, Solomon, Ṣāliḥ, and Lot, then addresses God’s unity in Lordship and the Resurrection. In (27:1), tilka includes the verses yet to be revealed in this chapter and those already revealed; its use for distant things indicates their loftiness and inaccessibility. The Book is called qurʾān because it is recited (maqruww), while mubīn, from ibānah, means showing or making manifest. The indefinite kitābin magnifies it: these revealed verses belong to a grand, recited Book, clear and unambiguous in its aims. Majmaʿ al-bayān reports that qurʾān and kitāb show that it is communicated by recitation and writing, and that mubīn likens it to an eloquent, expressive speaker.

For (27:2), hudā and bushrā are verbal nouns functioning as fāʿil, or are used instead of subjects for emphasis. Verse (27:3) describes righteous action through prayer and the poor-rate: prayer represents what pertains to God and the poor-rate what pertains to people, or respectively bodily and financial devotion. Such deeds are rightly placed and fruitful only with certainty in the hereafter; denying it annuls deeds: And (as to) those who reject Our signs and the meeting in the hereafter, their deeds are null (7:147). The repeated hum shows that this certainty is integral to believers’ status.

Regarding (27:4), ʿamah means taḥayyur, confusion or hesitation, and making deeds fair-seeming means making them attractive so that one is drawn to them. Since this world is a path and the hereafter its destination, those who disbelieve in the hereafter remain purposelessly wandering in the path while attached to their deeds. Their evil punishment in (27:5) includes worldly and otherworldly punishment. Al-Mizan suggests that they are the greatest losers because believers who sin have both good and evil deeds recorded and are requited for both, whereas disbelievers’ evil deeds remain while their good deeds are annulled.

In (27:6), talqiyah is close to talqīn, dictating or imparting. The indefinite names All-Wise and All-Knowing magnify God. The verse’s attribution of the Qur’an to God proves the Prophet’s mission, confirms the preceding teachings, and authenticates the prophetic narratives that follow. As issuing from wisdom, the Book cannot be negated or weakened; as issuing from knowledge, it neither lies in its statements nor errs in its judgments.
verses.2: Al-Mizan explains that hudā and bushrā are verbal nouns functioning as fāʿil, and may be used in place of subjects to convey emphasis.
verses.3: Al-Mizan explains that prayer and the poor-rate represent righteous deeds generally: respectively, what pertains to God and to people, or bodily and financial devotion. Such deeds are properly placed and bear fruit only with certainty in the hereafter; to deny it annuls one’s actions: And (as to) those who reject Our signs and the meeting in the hereafter, their deeds are null (7:147). The repeated hum indicates that certainty in the hereafter is integral to believers’ status and is expected of them.
verses.4: Al-Mizan explains that ʿamah means taḥayyur, confusion or hesitation, and that making deeds fair-seeming makes them attractive and draws a person to perform them. This world is a path and the hereafter its destination; therefore, those who deny the hereafter are left without purpose, wandering in this life while clinging to their deeds.
verses.5: Al-Mizan explains that the evil punishment includes both worldly and otherworldly punishment. It suggests that disbelievers are the greatest losers because, unlike sinful believers, whose good and evil deeds are both recorded and requited, their wrongdoings remain recorded while their good deeds are annulled.
verses.6: Al-Mizan explains that talqiyah is close to talqīn, dictating or imparting, and that the indefinite names All-Wise and All-Knowing express magnification. By attributing the Qur’an to God, the verse proves the Prophet’s mission, confirms the preceding teachings, and authenticates the prophetic narratives to follow. The Book comes from wisdom and therefore cannot be negated or weakened; it comes from knowledge and therefore neither lies in what it says nor errs in its judgments.
verses.7:
Al-Mizan explains that Moses’ “family” was his wife, Shuʿayb’s daughter. Majmaʿ al-bayān holds that the plural address may be used even for one person, since a lone companion offers the reassurance of a group in wilderness or fear; it is also possible that others, such as a servant or horseman, accompanied them.

Īnās means seeing, though ānastu has also been understood as sensing something with a feeling of familiarity or comfort. Shihāb here means a flame from a fire, and qabas is fire taken from a flame; iṣṭilāʾ with fire means warming oneself.

The context indicates that Moses and his family were cold, lost, and travelling in a very dark night. Seeing a distant fire, Moses went toward it, intending either to obtain news that would guide them or to bring back a firebrand for warmth. The fire apparently was visible only to him, since he mentioned it indefinitely rather than pointing it out. His repetition of “I will bring to you” perhaps distinguishes bringing information from bringing fire.
verses.8:
Al-Mizan explains mubārakah as the bestowal of abundant good. The parallel account—“So when he came to it, a voice uttered: O Moses! Surely I am your Lord. Therefore, take offyour shoes; surely you are in the sacred valley, Ṭuwā. And I have chosen you, so listen to what is revealed (20:11-13)”—indicates that Moses was among, or was himself, “whoever is about the fire”; his blessing was his sanctification and selection as a messenger.

Exegetes have offered several alternatives. Some identify the one in the fire with God, manifested through the fire surrounding the tree and speaking from it; on this view, “glory be to Allah, the Lord of the worlds” declares Him free of bodily properties, spatial location, and being affected by phenomena, rather than expressing Moses’ astonishment. Others identify those in and around the fire respectively as angels and Moses, or reverse them; identify the phrase with the blessed place of the tree, Moses, the surrounding Holy Land, and prophets descended from Abraham and Jacob; identify the one in the fire with God’s light and the one around it with Moses; or identify it with the tree surrounded by fire and angels around it glorifying God. Most of these interpretations, however, are not free from imposed personal opinion.
verses.9: Al-Mizan says that God identifies Himself to Moses so that he knows he is speaking directly with his Almighty Lord. This accords with: “It was called: O Moses! Surely I am your Lord, therefore put offyour shoes… (20:11-12).”
verses.10:
Al-Mizan explains that ihtizāz is rapid, violent movement; jānn is a small, swiftly moving snake; idbār is turning away; and taʿqīb is returning after fleeing. The revealing fāʾ in fa-lammā implies an omitted sequence: Moses cast down the staff, it became a moving serpent, and then he saw it moving.

The staff’s likeness here to a jānn and elsewhere to a thuʿbān, an enormous snake, is not contradictory. The former comparison concerns its swift movement, while the latter concerns another quality. Taken together, the staff became a huge, frightening serpent that moved with the speed of a small snake; neither comparison describes it in every respect.

It has been said that the staff took different miraculous forms on different occasions: a jānn at first—“So he cast it down, and lo! It was a serpent running (20:20)”—and an obvious thuʿbān before Pharaoh. Although this accords with the context, Al-Mizan finds a difficulty: either the staff did not become a ḥayyah, or the Qur’an compares a serpent to itself. Its own explanation, that the staff possessed qualities of both comparisons without being either in every respect, resolves this difficulty.

God’s words, “Fear not,” assure Moses against every feared evil, not merely fear of the staff. Complete security belongs to one at the threshold of divine nearness and in direct discourse with God. “Surely the messengers shall not fear in My presence” (27:10) means that the station of divine presence necessarily excludes every evil that can be feared; this is confirmed by “Surely you are of those who are secure (28:31).” Thus Moses need not fear because messengers, who are in God’s presence, are secure.

His flight from the terrifying, rapidly moving staff was an instinctive human response to danger when escape was his only protection, especially since his staff itself was the source of danger. God had commanded him only to cast it down, not to remain or refrain from fleeing. Such flight is not blameworthy timidity.

Although prophets and messengers fear nothing because they are always in their Lord’s presence, they attain this rank through God’s training and discipline, not through themselves. At Ṭūr, God first drew Moses near, chose him for divine speech, and granted him grace and messengership. “Fear not; surely you are of those who are secure” (28:31) and “Fear not; surely the messengers shall not fear in My presence” (27:10) therefore train and nurture Moses; they contain no rebuke.
verses.11:
Al-Mizan holds, most plausibly—and God knows best—that the verse makes an exception for sinners who repent. The security of the messengers might imply that unjust people should fear, but one who abandons sin, repents, and replaces evil with good is forgiven, receives mercy, and thereafter has no fear.

On this reading, illā is an unconnected exception: the unjust person is not included among the messengers, but the verse introduces a new statement. Ẓulm means every sin, and doing good after evil means repentance after disobedience and righteous deeds after wrongdoing. God forgives such a person’s injustice and has mercy on him.
verses.12: Al-Mizan notes that “without evil” has been interpreted as without leprosy (baraṣ). From the context, “among nine signs to Pharaoh and his people” describes the condition of both the staff and the hand: God gave Moses these two signs as two among the nine signs.
verses.13: Al-Mizan explains mubṣirah as clear and evident. By dismissing all the signs vaguely in the singular as hādhā—“this is clear enchantment”—they showed disparagement and disregard, without even caring to specify their number.
verses.14: Al-Mizan cites al-Rāghib: jaḥd is denying what one inwardly knows to be true, or affirming what one knows to be false. Istīqān and īqān both mean certainty and conviction.
verses.15: Al-Mizan explains that the indefinite form of ʿilman magnifies the knowledge given to David and Solomon; other verses likewise ascribe wisdom and judgment to David and wisdom and knowledge to both. Their praise acknowledges God’s preference over many believers. This preference may particularly be the superiority of their knowledge, as the context suggests, or an unrestricted preference embracing their special favors: David’s subjection of mountains and birds, softened iron, and kingship; and Solomon’s subjection of jinn, animals, birds, and wind, knowledge of birds’ language, and kingship. The verse’s unqualified wording supports the latter possibility. Their acknowledgment also evidences the chapter’s implied promise that God will soon give believers what delights them.
verses.16:
Al-Mizan holds that Solomon inherited David’s wealth and kingdom, not his prophethood or prophetic knowledge. Prophethood is not transferable, and although acquired mental knowledge may be transmitted in a sense, prophetic knowledge is a divine endowment rather than a product of mental activity. Non-prophets may receive knowledge from prophets through teaching, but a prophet does not inherit his knowledge from another person.

Solomon’s public declaration is an announcement of God’s favor, not self-glorification. Although some take the plurals in “We have been taught” and “We have been given” as a royal plural referring to Solomon and his retinue, the preceding discourse does not fully support this. Al-nās means all people, not merely rulers or scholars.

Manṭiq, like nuṭq, denotes the expression of an intended meaning. Though it is often used of humans, the Qur’an uses it more comprehensively for anything that conveys an intended meaning. This may be through extending a materially applied term to non-material cases, as with such Qur’anic terms as seeing and hearing, or because the term was originally general and became predominantly human in usage. Birds thus possess means of conveying their purposes, as animals make sounds in particular circumstances; but the birds’ language taught to Solomon was unquestionably subtler and broader than ordinary, commonly understood animal calls. It was an exclusive divine favor; the hoopoe’s ensuing discourse conveys extensive teachings concerning God, Satan, guidance, the kingdom of Sheba, and sun-worship; and human senses do not necessarily detect every animal sound or vibration, as the ant’s speech also indicates. The verse therefore refutes the claim that birds had no language of their own and that Solomon’s miracle was simply making them speak.

“We have been given all things” is qualified by its setting: Solomon and David received a sufficient share of every humanly beneficial blessing, including knowledge, prophethood, kingdom, judgment, and material and spiritual gifts, not literally every conceivable thing. “This is manifest grace” expresses gratitude and makes clear that these gifts are ascribed to God, not vaunted by Solomon; the view that God, rather than Solomon, speaks here conflicts with the verse’s flow.
verses.17:
Al-Mizan explains that ḥashr is mustering people and dispatching them forcibly for a task, while wazʿ is restraining, detaining, or preventing. Solomon’s hosts of jinn, men, and birds were assembled before him and kept from dispersing or intermingling, each group restrained in its place. The verse and its context show that particular groups of jinn and birds travelled with him, just as did his human host; they do not show that every jinn, human, and bird belonged to his army.

The commentary rejects al-Rāzī’s inferences that Solomon ruled the entire earth and that God temporarily made all birds, and the speaking ant, intelligent and legally responsible before restoring their former state. Its weaknesses need no exposition. Jinn are mentioned first because their subjection is most extraordinary; men precede birds because their subjection is also remarkable, and jinn and men are complementary.
verses.18: Al-Mizan explains that “until” marks the endpoint of Solomon’s journey with his hosts. When they came over the Valley of the Ants, an ant warned the others to enter their dwellings lest Solomon and his hosts crush them unknowingly. Ḥaṭm means breaking or crushing, and the plural refers to Solomon and his hosts. The verse shows that they were travelling on land; proposed locations for the valley do not determine its meaning.
verses.19:
Al-Mizan explains that tabassum is a smile preceding laughter, so the addition of ḍāḥikan conveys that Solomon’s smile nearly became laughter. His understanding of the ant does not conflict with his statement that he was taught the language of birds, for that statement does not deny his understanding of other animals. Speculations that this happened only once, that the ant was winged and therefore a bird, that its speech was an isolated miracle, or that Solomon knew only its inward thought by inspiration are unnecessary and contradicted by the context’s account of animal language.

Solomon’s delight at God’s favors—prophethood, kingdom, knowledge of animals’ language, and hosts of jinn, men, and birds—led him to ask for īzāʿ, that is, inspiration, to be grateful and to perform deeds pleasing to God. He names favors upon himself and his parents because their blessings were also blessings upon him through his existence: David received prophethood, kingship, wisdom, and decisive judgment, while Solomon’s mother was made David’s wife and the mother of a prophet. The supplication shows that she followed the straight path and belonged among those favored by God, as in (4:69).

His request to be inspired to righteous action is loftier than a request for tawfiq, which concerns the fitting availability of external means: inspiration is an inner drive toward felicity and salvation. It is therefore likely akin to the waḥy by which Abraham’s family were inspired to do good, namely aid by the Holy Spirit. Finally, his request for admission by mercy among God’s righteous servants concerns not merely righteous deeds but the essential righteousness of the soul, a higher state qualifying one for every divine honor. The requests rise in order from inspired righteous action to this essential righteousness. He asks God to inspire the former, but to make him one of the righteous in the latter sense, thereby seeking their exclusive blessings, foremost the station of servitude (ʿubūdiyyah).
verses.20: Al-Mizan explains that tafaqqud is inquiry directed to the loss or absence of something, unlike taʿahhud, which attends to a prior tie or condition. Solomon’s question, “How is it I see not the hoopoe?” first expresses surprise at his own failure to see it, as though he would not readily suspect the bird’s absence or disobedience. Only then does he raise the alternative that it may be among the absentees.
verses.21: Al-Mizan explains that the prefixed lām in each verb marks Solomon’s emphatic vow. He sets three possible outcomes for the hoopoe: severe punishment, slaughter, or production of a clear proof (sulṭān mubīn). The first two entail its doom, whereas a clear justification secures its safety.
verses.22: Al-Mizan notes two possible antecedents for “he tarried not long”: Solomon, in continuity with the preceding verses, or the hoopoe, in view of what follows. Iḥāṭah means full knowledge, and the hoopoe’s bringing of certain news explains its claim to have comprehended what Solomon had not. Sheba was Yemen’s capital, nabaʾ is important news, and yaqīn means doubtless. The concise verse implies a brief wait, the hoopoe’s return, Solomon’s reproach for its absence, and its answer that it had brought indisputable, important news from Sheba. Some exegetes say its opening claim was intended to draw Solomon’s attention and calm his anger.
verses.23: Al-Mizan explains that “them” denotes the people of Sheba and its surrounding region. The queen’s being given “of every thing” means the resources of a great empire—prudence, authority, power, lands, treasures, armies, and obedient subjects—not every conceivable thing. The hoopoe singles out her mighty throne from among these marks of her vast kingdom.
verses.24: Al-Mizan identifies the queen and her people as sun-worshipping idolaters. Satan made their acts of worship besides Allah—such as prostration and other acts seeking their gods’ favor—appear fair to them, thereby turning them from “the way,” God’s way of worshipping Him alone. Its unqualified expression indicates that this is the only path intrinsically suited to humankind’s fiṭrah, indeed to creation as a whole. Since they were turned from the only true way, they consequently did not go aright.
verses.25:
Al-Mizan explains the common reading allā as “that they do not,” an exposition of the deeds Satan made fair-seeming: their failure to prostrate to God. The proposed reading li-allā, “so that they would not,” is only an alternative requiring an omitted lām of purpose.

Al-khabʾ is what is hidden and imperceptibly enclosed. “Who brings forth what is hidden in the heavens and the earth” is metaphorical: things lie hidden beneath the layers of non-existence, and God brings them into existence. This resembles fiṭr, splitting non-existence to bring things forth. A literal meaning is also possible but requires an explanation beyond the present discussion. The interpretation that khabʾ means the unseen and that bringing it forth means merely knowing it is weak because it abandons the apparent senses of the terms. While the received wording addresses “what you hide and what you make manifest,” the widely transmitted third-person reading, “what they hide and what they make manifest,” is preferable in meaning.

The verse argues that the sun is revered only for benefits God placed in it within the ordered universe. God, however, creates all things from non-existence into existence, establishes and directs that order, including the sun, and knows what people conceal and disclose. The sun cannot even know that it is worshipped. Therefore God alone, rather than the sun or anything else, is worthy of prostration and reverence.
verses.26: Al-Mizan holds that the hoopoe remains the speaker and explicitly draws the conclusion of its preceding argument against the people’s false belief. “There is no god but He” establishes monotheism in worship, while “the Lord of the Mighty Throne” establishes that God directs all affairs, for a king’s throne denotes the central seat from which he governs his kingdom. The parallel with the queen’s “mighty throne” may have prompted, or helped prompt, Solomon to have her throne brought before him, so that every glory might be humbled before his Lord’s magnificence.
verses.27: Al-Mizan explains that Solomon neither affirmed the hoopoe’s report without evidence nor denied it without grounds. He deferred judgment and declared that he would test whether it had spoken truthfully or was among the liars.
verses.28: Al-Mizan explains that Solomon instructed the hoopoe to carry his letter to the Queen of Sheba and her commanders, cast it to them, withdraw to a place from which it could observe them, and watch the response they exchanged in discussing it. The hāʾ of fa-alqih is hāʾ al-sakt, pronounced as a pause in every recitation. The suggestion that the final two instructions are in reverse sequence—meaning that the hoopoe should first observe their answer and then return—is implausible.
verses.29:
Al-Mizan supplies the implied sequence: the hoopoe took Solomon’s letter to the Queen of Sheba, cast it to her, and she read it before addressing her chiefs. She calls it karīm because it is from Solomon and because it is in the name of Allah, the Beneficent, the Merciful. Her knowledge of Solomon’s great dominion explains the first reason. The second is also fitting because idolaters, including sun-worshippers, acknowledged God as Lord of lords, though they did not worship Him; the Sabeans exalted His attributes, interpreting knowledge, power, life, and mercy as negations of their opposites.

The commentary rejects the view that “It is from Solomon” begins a new answer to an implied question and that “it is in the name of Allah” begins a verbatim quotation of the letter. On that view, an at the opening of (27:31) becomes redundant unless it is given a contrived grammatical interpretation. The many proposed reasons for calling the letter honorable—its seal, handwriting, unusual delivery, or supposed heavenly origin—likewise arise from this error. Both instances of innahu in (27:30) instead explain why the letter is honorable, while an in (27:31) descriptively introduces its purport rather than a direct quotation: it begins with God’s name and commands them not to be arrogant before Solomon but to come to him in submission.
verses.30:
Al-Mizan supplies the implied sequence: the hoopoe took Solomon’s letter to the Queen of Sheba, cast it to her, and she read it before addressing her chiefs. She calls it karīm because it is from Solomon and because it is in the name of Allah, the Beneficent, the Merciful. Her knowledge of Solomon’s great dominion explains the first reason. The second is also fitting because idolaters, including sun-worshippers, acknowledged God as Lord of lords, though they did not worship Him; the Sabeans exalted His attributes, interpreting knowledge, power, life, and mercy as negations of their opposites.

The commentary rejects the view that “It is from Solomon” begins a new answer to an implied question and that “it is in the name of Allah” begins a verbatim quotation of the letter. On that view, an at the opening of (27:31) becomes redundant unless it is given a contrived grammatical interpretation. The many proposed reasons for calling the letter honorable—its seal, handwriting, unusual delivery, or supposed heavenly origin—likewise arise from this error. Both instances of innahu in (27:30) instead explain why the letter is honorable, while an in (27:31) descriptively introduces its purport rather than a direct quotation: it begins with God’s name and commands them not to be arrogant before Solomon but to come to him in submission.
verses.31:
Al-Mizan holds that an is explanatory, introducing the purport of Solomon’s letter: “Do not exalt yourselves against me, and come to me in submission.” The alternative that an is maṣdariyyah and lā merely negative is implausible, since it needlessly requires an omitted subject or predicate and ungrammatically joins a declarative clause to the imperative “come to me.”

The command forbids haughtiness and calls for islām in its literal sense of submission and obedience to Solomon, not īmān or Islam in the technical sense of faith in God. Had that technical sense been meant, the prohibition would have concerned exalting themselves against God. Yet political submission to Solomon, who was both prophet and king, entailed belief in God; the queen’s submission to him ultimately led to her submission to God: I submit with Solomon to Allah, the Lord of the worlds (27:44).
verses.32: Al-Mizan explains that iftāʾ is giving an opinion, qaṭʿ an affair is deciding it firmly, and shahādah here means presence. The Queen of Sheba asks her chiefs to advise her concerning Solomon’s letter because she does not govern autocratically: she makes decisions and decrees through consultation in their presence. This is the second part of her address, following her report of the letter, its arrival, and its message.
verses.33: Al-Mizan explains quwwah here as military strength and baʾs as courage and ferocity in action. The queen’s chiefs first reassure her that their forces and valor leave them unafraid even of Solomon, then return the decision to her: she may command as she wishes, and they will obey.
verses.34: Al-Mizan explains the Queen’s warning: a king’s entry ruins a town by destruction, burning, and demolition, and abases its nobles through killing, capture, exile, deportation, and tyranny. Her chiefs’ appeal to strength and mighty prowess apparently shows an inclination to war; she criticizes war implicitly before stating her plan. Because war ends in one side’s victory, with ruined towns and humiliated leaders, prudence counsels peace with a powerful enemy while conciliation remains possible, unless war becomes unavoidable. She will instead send a gift, have messengers investigate the signs of Solomon’s prophethood and kingdom, and decide between war and peace from their report. Grammatically, her adjective “abased,” rather than a verb meaning “abase,” indicates not merely an event but the nobles’ condition of being drenched in abasement. Likewise, “and thus they (always) do” moves from the initial ruin and abasement to their persistence. The commentary rejects treating that final clause as a divine interjection, because the verse gives no evidence that the Queen’s speech has ended.
verses.35: Al-Mizan explains that the queen’s plural reference to “them” denotes Solomon and his retinue. By avoiding Solomon’s name, she displays royal pride and haughtiness, while also recognizing that his affairs are conducted through assistants, hosts, and subjects. She proposes sending a gift and awaiting her messengers’ report before acting according to the circumstances. Though the messengers were a group, one headed them, as Solomon later addresses a single person: irjiʿ ilayhim.
verses.36:
Al-Mizan takes the arriving subject to be either the gift or its bearer. Solomon’s question is a rebuke addressed grammatically to the messengers but intended also for those in Sheba who sent them; the offered help was from the sender, not merely from the present delegation. The indefinite mālin underscores the insignificance of their wealth. God’s gift to Solomon—his prophethood, kingdom, and wealth—is better than theirs, so the gift is worthless to him.

Solomon further rebukes them for exulting in the gift itself, regarding and admiring a worldly offering that is paltry beside God’s favor. The alternative reading that “your present” means gifts presented to them, over which they rejoice because they love wealth, is unlikely.
verses.37:
Al-Mizan explains that Solomon addresses the head of the delegation, while the plural refers to the Queen of Sheba and her people. Qibal means power or ability to resist, and bihā refers to Sheba. The emphatic lām marks a vow: Solomon threatens to come with hosts they cannot oppose in their land and to expel them from it abased and ignominious.

Their gift, sent instead of complying with his order to come in submission, signified refusal and anticipated resistance. Thus the condition is implicit: he would send armies and expel them only if they persisted in resisting. The verse’s context also shows that Solomon rejected and returned their gift.
verses.38: Al-Mizan explains that, after rejecting the gift and returning the messengers, Solomon told his chiefs that the queen and her people would soon come in submission and asked who could bring her throne beforehand. Its arrival before them would manifest the great power God gave him and serve as a clear prophetic miracle through which they would submit to God.
verses.39: Al-Mizan explains ʿifrīt as an audacious, wicked, evil jinn. Its ātīka bihi is most fittingly an active participial claim, “I am a bringer of it to you,” though it may also mean “I will bring it”; the former accords with the following nominal assertion of settled strength and trustworthiness. The jinn claims it can bring the throne before Solomon rises from his place, without difficulty in lifting or carrying it, and that it will faithfully perform the task.
verses.40:
Al-Mizan holds that the one possessing “a knowledge of the Book” was a human being, as the contrast with the jinn indicates. Narrations from the Imams of Ahl al-Bayt identify him as Āṣif b. Barkhiyā, Asaph son of Berachiah, Solomon’s vizier and successor; claims that he was Khiḍr, Gabriel, Solomon, or merely a man possessing the Greatest Name have no supporting evidence. The verse’s unconnected transition stresses this scholar’s importance, while the indefinite “a knowledge” magnifies a knowledge beyond ordinary description.

“The Book” may mean the genus of heavenly scriptures or the Guarded Tablet (al-lawḥ al-maḥfūẓ). His knowledge from it enabled the throne’s transport in less than the time between sighting an object and its image becoming known to the viewer. Reports that specify verbal formulas of the Greatest Name are not indicated by the verse. Moreover, the commentary rejects the idea that a Name capable of affecting all things could be a mere spoken formula or a mental concept. If such a Name exists, it is an external divine reality, while a word indicating it is only “the name of the name” (ism al-ism). The verse instead establishes that this man had such knowledge and connection with God that, when he turned to his Lord and asked, his request would certainly be granted if God willed. This was not intellectual knowledge acquired through learning.

The statement is addressed to Solomon, who asked for the throne, not to the ʿifrīt; the contrary interpretation, which makes Solomon himself the speaker in order to demonstrate prophetic superiority, does not fit the context. The omission between the man’s offer and Solomon’s seeing the throne beside him conveys the act’s instantaneous speed. Solomon calls the throne’s actual appearance before him, not a pre-existing ability to bring it, a grace from his Lord that tests whether he is grateful or ungrateful. Gratitude benefits its bearer alone, while kufr here means ingratitude, and God is Self-sufficient and Honored.
verses.41: Al-Mizan explains tankīr as altering something so that it cannot be recognized, the opposite of taʿrīf. Solomon apparently ordered the queen’s throne altered as she and her chiefs were about to meet him. As bringing it had displayed a manifest sign of his prophethood, altering it tested her intellect and whether she would follow the right way or fail to do so.
verses.42:
Al-Mizan explains that the question put to the queen on Solomon’s behalf was a test, not a request for information. Rather than ask directly whether it was her throne, they asked whether it resembled hers, obscuring the matter through tankīr. Her “It is as it were the same” means that it was the same, but expresses her initial judgment cautiously rather than asserting what she had not fully verified.

The continuation, “we were given the knowledge before it, and we were submissive,” is her own speech. “Before it” may refer either to the throne’s transport or to the present sight of it. She recognizes the throne as an allusion to the extraordinary power God had granted Solomon and says that she and her people already knew of that power, so the sign was unnecessary as a reminder. Their submission here is obedience to Solomon, not yet submission to God. The alternative attributions of this statement to Solomon, his people, or a queen merely claiming prior knowledge that the throne had been moved are implausible.
verses.43: Al-Mizan explains ṣaddahā as the queen’s being prevented or turned away from submission to God by what she worshipped besides Him, namely the sun. Her earlier statement that “we were submissive” (27:42) concerned political obedience to Solomon, whereas her submission to God occurs later in her testimony: I submit with Solomon to Allah, the Lord of the worlds (27:44). Her idolatry prevented that submission because she belonged to an unbelieving people and followed them in their unbelief.
verses.44:
Al-Mizan records three possible senses of al-ṣarḥ: a palace, an elevated building overlooking others, or a broad unroofed space. Lujjah is a great expanse of water, mumarrad means smoothly refined, and qawārīr means glass. One of Solomon’s servants apparently invited the queen to enter; mistaking the glass-covered floor for water, she lifted her garment to avoid wetting it. Solomon then explained that it was a glass palace.

After the hoopoe’s appearance, the return of her gifts, and the transport of her throne, the splendor of this palace left her without doubt that these were signs of Solomon’s prophethood rather than a scheme. She consequently confessed that she had wronged herself by failing to serve God from the outset, or by delaying conversion after seeing these signs. Her declaration that she submitted with Solomon to Allah, the Lord of the worlds, moves from directly addressing “My Lord” to an explicit testimony of tawḥīd. “With Solomon” means submission of the same kind as his—pure monotheism—and “Lord of the worlds” affirms that no being in any realm has another lord. Unity in Lordship entails unity in worship, which polytheists deny.

Al-Mizan then notes that the Qur’an presents selected episodes of Solomon’s life: his inheritance from David, his vast kingdom and rule over jinn, birds, and wind, his knowledge of birds’ language, the body placed on his throne, the horses offered to him, his correct judgment concerning the sheep and tillage, the ant, the hoopoe and Queen of Sheba, and his death. It repeatedly praises him as an excellent servant frequently returning to God, a prophet granted knowledge and judgment, and one of the guided prophets.

The commentary contrasts this with the Old Testament’s account, which broadly describes his kingdom, wealth, wisdom, and visit from the Queen of Sheba, but alleges that he later worshipped his wives’ idols and that he was born from David’s unlawful union with Uriah’s wife after David arranged Uriah’s death. The Qur’an exonerates him from the first calumny by counting him among guided, infallible prophets and declaring: And Solomon disbelieved not (2:102). It also clears his mother from the second accusation: his prayer for favors bestowed on himself and his parents indicates that she was on the straight path, among those favored by God.
verses.45: Al-Mizan explains that the plural yakhtaṣimūna, despite farīqān being dual, refers to Thamūd as a whole, while fa-idhā marks their sudden, unexpected division. Though Ṣāliḥ, their relative, called them to serve Allah and they should have been united in faith, they split into believers and disbelievers, each disputing the truth. Perhaps this quarrel is the one described in (7:75-76): lower-status people believed in Ṣāliḥ, whereas the proud chiefs (al-mustakbirūn) denied him, and the remaining al-mustaḍʿafūn followed their chiefs.
verses.46: Al-Mizan explains that Ṣāliḥ rebuked his people for eagerly demanding punishment rather than seeking the good of divine mercy. Mercy follows belief and asking Allah’s forgiveness. The rebuke appears to have come after they hamstrung the she-camel and challenged him, “O Ṣāliḥ! Bring us what you threatened us with, if you are one of the messengers” (7:77). He therefore called them to believe and repent, so that Allah might show them mercy and remove the promised punishment, “a promise not to be belied” (11:65).
verses.47:
Al-Mizan explains that taṭayyur is taking something as an evil omen, so called because birds were commonly used for this purpose; ṭāʾir consequently denotes one’s allotted evil and misfortune. Ṣāliḥ’s people blamed him, the believers, and his followers for the hardships coinciding with his call, and used this as their reason for refusing faith and forgiveness.

Ṣāliḥ replies that their share of evil—the punishment their deeds deserve—rests with Allah, not with him or his followers, who have no power to cause their tribulations. Their omen is their book of deeds, and they are instead being tested through good and evil so that believers are distinguished from disbelievers and the obedient from the disobedient.

Some exegetes hold that ṭāʾir includes whatever brings good or evil, and thus identify it with the Guarded Book, al-lawḥ al-maḥfūẓ, citing And We have made every man’s bird of omen (ṭāʾirah) cling to his neck, and We will bring forth a book to him on the Day of Resurrection (17:13). Al-Mizan rejects this, since Read your book; your own self is sufficient as a reckoner against you this day (17:14) shows that it is the book of deeds, not the book of decree. It also finds more plausible the interpretation of “you are a people who are tried” as being tested, rather than being punished.
verses.48: Al-Mizan notes differing lexical definitions of rahṭ, but explains that here it means persons in the plural and functions as the specification of “nine.” Thus the group who mutually pledged their plot consisted of nine men.
verses.49:
Al-Mizan explains that taqāsum means mutually vowing, and tabyīt means harming someone at night. The corrupt group swore by Allah to kill Ṣāliḥ and his ahl by night; ahl may here mean his wife and children. When his heir sought blood-money, they intended to deny witnessing the destruction of his family and to insist that they were truthful. Their denial of witnessing his family’s death also entails their denial of witnessing his own death.

The conjunction in “and we are most surely truthful” adds this assertion to their intended statement to the heir. Al-Mizan rejects as contrived the view that it is ḥāliyyah, meaning that they would speak truthfully because, although they did not see the family perish separately, they saw Ṣāliḥ and his family perish together.
verses.50: Al-Mizan identifies their plot as their mutual pledge to attack Ṣāliḥ and his family, and Allah’s counter-plot as His decree to destroy them.
verses.51: Al-Mizan explains tadmīr as destruction and obliteration. The plural pronouns refer to the rahṭ, whose plot brought Allah’s punitive counter-plot and thus ended in the destruction of them and all their people.
verses.52: Al-Mizan explains khāwiyah as empty and vacant: their houses lay fallen and deserted because of their injustice, a sign for those who know. A translator’s note adds that their people shared in the plot through approving it, citing Nahj al-balāghah, Sermon 201.
verses.53: Al-Mizan presents the verse as glad tidings that believers will be delivered, and adds that taqwā shields īmān. Thus, “the end is for those who guard (against evil)” (7:128), and “the (good) end is for guarding (against evil)” (20:132).
verses.54: Al-Mizan reports that some exegetes take the conjunction to continue “We sent…” (27:45), implying, “We certainly sent Lot”; it may instead join Lot’s whole account to Ṣāliḥ’s, implying, “And remember Lot.” Al-fāḥishah, an extremely reprehensible act, here means sodomy. “While you see” means that they committed it while seeing one another, as in: And you commit evil deeds in your assemblies? (29:29). The proposed meaning that they inwardly recognized its indecency is a strained reading beyond the textual and contextual evidence.
verses.55: Al-Mizan explains that the question is rhetorical, denying and rebuking their lustful approach to men rather than women. Its two emphatic particles, inna and lām in innakum la-taʾtūna, mark the act as so reprehensible that no one could approve it; the verse itself thus explains the preceding “indecency.” Tajhalūna, being present tense, denotes their persistence in ignorant conduct, so that rebuke is futile because they will not desist. Although “a people who act ignorantly” would ordinarily use the third person, the second-person tajhalūna treats the effect as the cause: they are a people characterized by ignorance and therefore act ignorantly.
verses.56: Al-Mizan explains that Lot’s people demanded the expulsion of his followers because they kept away from this act; calling them people who “keep pure” was derisive mockery.
verses.57: Al-Mizan takes ahlihi to mean Lot’s household specifically, supported by: But We did not find therein save a (single) house of those who submitted (51:36). His wife was excluded from their deliverance because God included her among those left for punishment.
verses.58: Al-Mizan states that the rain sent upon them was stones of baked clay, as in: And We rained down upon them stones of baked clay (15:74). The indefinite maṭaran indicates a distinctive kind of rain, conveying the greatness and immensity of this punishment.
verses.59:
Al-Mizan explains that, after recounting God’s customary treatment of believing and disbelieving nations, the verse turns to praise, peace upon God’s chosen servants, and the declaration of His oneness. Though it effectively completes the preceding discussion, it is not grammatically presented as its formal conclusion.

All praise belongs ultimately to God, since creation and the direction of all affairs return to Him; by wisdom He bestows every good, and by power performs every gracious act. The command to send peace upon His chosen servants is likewise part of what the Prophet is ordered to say. Such peace requires inwardly abandoning resistance to them, because they bear divine guidance and its fruits; it therefore implicitly commands readiness to accept their guidance and its implications, much like: These are they whom Allah guided, therefore follow their guidance (6:90).

The final rhetorical question requires acknowledgment that God is better than the associated gods. Those gods neither create nor direct any affair for which praise is due, and possess no good to grant their worshippers.
verses.60:
Al-Mizan explains that ḥadāʾiq means walled or enclosed gardens, while dhāt bahjah describes the gardens collectively as possessing a beautiful, delightful appearance. The singular expression treats the gardens as a unit rather than describing each garden separately.

The opening am is disconnected from the preceding question and means “rather” or “nay.” The verse leaves one side of its rhetorical comparison unstated: is the One who created heaven and earth, sent rain for people’s benefit, and caused delightful gardens to grow—trees which they cannot make grow—better, or what they associate with Him? Its question, “Is there a god with Allah?”, is thus censure and rebuke.

The shift from third-person reference to direct address in “sent down for you” intensifies the rebuke of the polytheists. God confronts them with signs, rejects their association of partners, and reproaches them for turning from Him. “They are people who deviate” means that they turn from truth and from God to falsehood and others; some exegetes take yaʿdilūna to mean that they make others equal to Him. The return to third-person address indicates that persuasion is futile because they persist in deviation.
verses.61:
Al-Mizan explains that the verse continues the unstated rhetorical comparison: is the One who made the earth stable so that it does not shake people, made rivers flow through its openings, fixed mountains upon it, and set a barrier between two seas to prevent their mixing, better than the beings associated with Him?

Qarāran denotes the earth’s settled stability; khilālahā refers to its gaps or openings; rawāsī are fixed mountains; and ḥājizan is a barrier between two things. The closing question and rebuke are like those in the preceding verse: there is no god alongside Allah, yet most of them do not know.
verses.62:
Al-Mizan holds that God’s answering of al-muḍtarr concerns every genuinely distressed caller who has grasped the reality of supplication. True petition does not arise while a person still relies on alternative recourses. The additional condition, “when he calls upon Him,” requires calling upon God alone: when the caller is cut off from apparent means and the heart clings solely to its Lord. If the heart is attached to means, whether alone or together with God, it is not truly calling upon God alone.

Accordingly, every genuine supplication directed exclusively to God is answered, and the evil that occasioned it is removed. This accords with: And your Lord says: Call upon Me, I will answer you (40:60), and: And when My servants ask you concerning Me, then surely I am very near; I answer the prayer of the suppliant when he calls on Me (2:186). Al-Mizan rejects the view that al-muḍtarr refers only to distressed people as a class rather than to each individual, since these verses do not allow that some genuine calls remain unanswered. In acute distress, human fiṭrah recognizes that the direction of affairs belongs to God and turns sincerely to Him. Seeking apparent means merely in hope of their benefit is instead “mental supplication,” based on speculation, as distinct from this instinctive and natural supplication; even it contains an underlying search for means in the absolute sense, which does not fail.

The commentary also rejects limiting “the distressed one” to a sinner seeking forgiveness: this neither solves the issue of total inclusion nor has grounds for restricting the unrestricted term al-muḍtarr. It further rejects qualifying the present promise by the divine will mentioned in: So He clears away that for which you pray if He wills (6:41). That verse concerns calls that may be real or unreal: the Hour cannot be removed, while chastisement is removed through sincere repentance and belief, not by a merely verbal plea made as a device for escape. Thus God wills to remove the requested evil where the request is real and believing; this differs from verses concerning a genuine call to God alone.

“He will make you vicegerents in the earth” refers, in this context, to the vicegerency granted to humankind: its dominion over the earth and use of its resources for life and survival. The evil removed is therefore what obstructs or restricts that earthly life and dominion. If duʿāʾ is understood broadly, rather than as verbal request alone, all powers and blessings given to people are instances of their call being answered and their evil removed; this completes their vicegerency. Al-Mizan finds this more suited to the context than interpreting the verse as believers succeeding disbelievers in their towns, since the address is to disbelievers, or as people merely succeeding former nations.

“Little is it that you mind” rebukes the disbelievers. The alternative reading yadhdhakkarūna is considered more plausible because, like the endings of the surrounding verses, it shifts the address back to the Prophet.
verses.63: Al-Mizan explains that “utter darkness of the land and the sea” figuratively means the darkness of night on land and sea. The winds are glad tidings because they herald rain, which is the mercy meant here. The verse asks whether any god is with Allah and declares Him exalted above their associations.
verses.64:
Al-Mizan explains that origination is the beginning of creation’s existence, and reproduction is its return to existence at the Resurrection. The verse therefore argues against polytheism by the Resurrection, despite the polytheists’ denial of it, because the Qur’an treats it as established by decisive proofs. The alternative explanation—that origination and reproduction mean successive members of a species being created after one another—does not readily follow from the verse’s apparent meaning.

The verse also implies that existence is never extinguished. What God originates returns to Him through His returning of it; apparent extermination is only its absence from our possession or sight. Consequently, disputes over iʿādat al-maʿdūm, including whether annihilated substances can be restored, do not concern resurrection. Resurrection is not the restoration of something annihilated, but creatures’ return to their originating Lord without extinction or termination of existence.

Sustenance from heaven and earth denotes God’s direction of human affairs between origination and return, through heavenly means such as rain and earthly means that nourish humanity. Creation and tadbīr are one reality belonging to and dependent on God alone. Since ulūhiyyah follows from lordship, and a lord directs the affairs of what he owns, worship is connected with directing affairs: it expresses gratitude for blessing or seeks protection from punishment. Thus no being invoked besides God is truly divine. The command, “Say: Bring your proof if you are truthful,” challenges the polytheists to establish a divine role for their gods in directing the universe; their inability to do so shows that all creation and direction belong to God alone.
verses.65:
Al-Mizan explains that this is a second argument against the divinity of the polytheists’ gods. None in the heavens or earth knows the unseen, including the angels, jinn, and human saints whom they take as gods; nor do they know when they themselves will be raised. Were they gods directing created affairs, they would know the Hour, since resurrection and requital belong to that direction.

The statement that none knows the unseen but Allah independently negates their gods’ divinity and affirms God’s alone. Their ignorance of the time of resurrection is then the clearest and most important instance of such unseen knowledge. Both occurrences of “they” refer to all those in the heavens and earth, not specifically to the polytheists; otherwise the argument against the alleged gods would be incomplete. Al-Mizan rejects the contrary view that avoids a shift in the referent of pronouns between this verse and the next, since such a shift is unobjectionable where context indicates it.
verses.66:
Al-Mizan explains iddāraka as tadāraka: the successive exhaustion of something until none remains. Their knowledge has been exhausted in worldly concerns, leaving them without knowledge of the hereafter. Thus they are far from being able to know the Hour: they lack knowledge of the hereafter itself, doubt it when it reaches their hearts, and are finally blind to it because God has blinded the eyes of their hearts from accepting its truth.

The repeated bal marks this ascending sequence of ignorance: first, no knowledge of the hereafter as though they had never heard of it; then doubt after hearing of it; then a blindness not brought about by their own volition, which prevents understanding its realities. Al-Mizan rejects the interpretation that tadāruk means the completion of their certain knowledge through perfected proofs, since it does not fit the subsequent progression to doubt and blindness.
verses.67: Al-Mizan explains that the disbelievers argue against resurrection from its apparent improbability: how can they, after becoming dust, and their fathers as well, be brought forth from the earth again as complete human beings?
verses.68: Al-Mizan explains that the polytheists regard resurrection as improbable because they and their fathers had long been promised it by this Prophet and earlier prophets. Since they suppose that, if it were true, it would already have occurred, they dismiss it as fabricated stories and superstitious fables of the ancients.
verses.69:
Al-Mizan reports one exegetical reading of the command to travel through the earth as a warning to the polytheists: they should observe the ruined dwellings and deserted towns of guilty deniers who rejected their prophets’ warning about resurrection. Calling them “sinners” rather than “deniers” also subtly admonishes believers to avoid sin.

The commentary considers it also possible that the verse argues for the hereafter. The exterminating punishment of earlier sinners shows that wrongdoing is not disregarded: deeds are preserved for their doers and entail accountability. Since deeds, especially righteous ones, are not all recompensed in this world, another abode is required—the hereafter. This reading is supported by “the end of the sinners”; had the point merely been to threaten those who denied the messengers, “the deniers” would have been expected instead.
verses.70: Al-Mizan explains that the verse consoles the Prophet: he must not grieve over their persistent disbelief and defiance, nor be distressed by their schemes to refute his call and turn people from God’s way. They remain under God’s watch, cannot frustrate Him, and will certainly be requited. The clause concerning their plotting interprets and specifies the command not to grieve.
verses.71: Al-Mizan explains that “this promise” apparently denotes the threatened punishment in both this world and the hereafter, as the context indicates.
verses.72:
Al-Mizan explains radifa lakum as indicating the nearness of punishment. Some take the lām in lakum as emphatic, so that the promise is following them and will soon reach them; others hold that radifa takes lām in its transitive use. In either case, the expression signifies that punishment has drawn near.

“Some part of that which you seek to hasten on” is worldly punishment preceding the hereafter. In demanding the decisive judgment promised by God, the polytheists were pressing for what entailed their own punishment. Some suggest that it concerns the punishment at Badr.

The commentary rejects the claim that ʿasā and similar expressions must mean certainty when used by God, on the ground that hope would imply divine ignorance. Expressions of expectation may instead be relative to the context or audience. Because the reply is placed on the Prophet’s tongue, ʿasā conveys his expectation: he says that punishment may have drawn near. Tafsīr Abī al-Suʿūd reports that rulers’ use of words such as ʿasā, laʿalla, and sawfa can function like definite statements by others, displaying that their allusions carry the force of explicit speech; Al-Mizan calls this plausible. The verse thus warns that the worldly punishment they seek to hasten may be close and will lead them toward punishment in the hereafter.
verses.73: Al-Mizan explains that, amid warnings of punishment, God’s grace consists in withholding punishment from people even though they deserve it for their conduct. Rather than thank Him for this forbearance, most of them demand that the punishment be hastened.
verses.74: Al-Mizan explains that the postponement of their punishment is not due to God’s ignorance of their disbelief, defiance, or deserts. He knows both what their breasts conceal and what they outwardly manifest. Moreover, everything hidden in heaven and earth, in any respect, is written and preserved in a clear book.
verses.75: Al-Mizan explains that the postponement of their punishment is not due to God’s ignorance of their disbelief, defiance, or deserts. He knows both what their breasts conceal and what they outwardly manifest. Moreover, everything hidden in heaven and earth, in any respect, is written and preserved in a clear book.
verses.76:
Al-Mizan explains that these verses strengthen believers, console the Prophet, and prepare for the affirmation of the truth of his call. The Qur’an declares to the Children of Israel most matters in which they differ: its stories clarify their disputes concerning the prophets, including the truth concerning the Christ, and it also sets out the true beliefs and laws over which they differ.

For believers, the Qur’an is guidance to truth and mercy because it reassures their hearts and makes their faith firm. Judgment between those who differ belongs to God alone. He is Mighty, so none can overcome His command, and Knowing, so His judgment is free of ignorance and error. The Prophet should therefore be content with God as judge, entrust judgment to Him, and leave the punishment of the polytheists to Him rather than grieve over their plotting.

verses.79:
Al-Mizan presents these verses as the conclusion to the Prophet’s charge concerning the polytheists and the disagreements of the Children of Israel. Their affair belongs to God, not to him. He must therefore rely on God as his guardian and sufficiency, without fear, because he stands upon the clear truth.

The command is justified because the Prophet cannot guide those likened to the dead, deaf, and blind. He cannot make the dead hear, make the deaf hear the call while they turn away retreating, or guide the blind out of their error. He can make the message reach only those who believe in God’s communications, submit to Him, and confirm what the signs establish by yielding to sure proofs. The qualification “when they go back retreating” perhaps indicates that, if they did not turn away, some form of sign language might at least make them understand.

Here ismāʿ, making one hear, means guiding. The āyāt are proofs for tawḥīd and the other religious truths that follow from it. Whoever uses sound judgment and reason upon the true proofs in God’s signs in the horizons and souls, understands them and submits in belief and obedience, is not among the dead or among those whose hearing and sight have been sealed.

verses.82:
Al-Mizan explains that the pronouns initially address the Meccan polytheists hostile to the Prophet, but the ruling extends to all members of his community, later generations included, since they share one divine call. The falling of al-qawl means that the divine word becomes applicable and determined against them; unlike ḥaqqa al-qawl, the expression waqaʿa al-qawl ʿalayhim particularly identifies those upon whom it falls.

The commentary interprets this word through: We will soon show them Our signs in the Universe and in their own souls, until it will become quite clear to them that it is the truth (41:53). It is the coming of extraordinary, compelling signs, not the ordinary signs continually visible in heaven and earth. Such signs come after people have failed to believe through the ordinary signs. Their established disbelief, indicated by kānū, is the reason the word falls upon them; “Our signs” in this clause are the ordinary signs. The recitation inna is preferable to anna because it directly makes their disbelief an explanatory justification for the word’s falling, without positing an omitted lām.

The creature, dābbah, brought forth from the earth is one of these extraordinary signs. Its emergence must be supernatural, such as a coming to life after death or something similar. Dābbah can include humans and animals: if it is human, its speech is ordinary, while if it is an animal, both its emergence and speech are extraordinary. The Qur’an provides no further explanation of its identity, qualities, manner of emergence, or words; the intended expression is deliberately obscure and mysterious.

Thus, when people have lost the capacity and opportunity to believe through reasoning and taking lessons, God will show them extraordinary signs that compel recognition of the truth, including a creature from the earth that speaks to them. Al-Mizan rejects the numerous detailed proposals about the creature’s nature, speech, time, place, and repeated emergence as unsupported contrivances.
verses.83:
Al-Mizan takes yawma as governed by an implied “remember.” A fawj is a rapidly moving group, and īzāʿ means holding a group so that those ahead and behind assemble. The ḥashr is a posthumous gathering, since parties from every nation cannot be gathered simultaneously in worldly life. The first min is partitive; the second may be partitive or explanatory.

The signs rejected are unrestricted signs of the divine origin and end, including prophets, Imams, and divine scriptures, but not the Resurrection itself or its final events. They cannot mean Qur’anic verses alone, for the gathering includes parties from every nation, whereas the Qur’an belongs only to one community. The argument that the following verse concerns signs requiring reflection therefore does not establish that āyāt means only Qur’anic verses.

The verse apparently does not describe the universal Resurrection gathering, because it gathers only a party from each nation, whereas: And We will gather them and leave not any one of them behind (18:47) describes the Resurrection as universal. Nor is it plausibly a special post-Resurrection gathering for punishment: the verse gives no indication of punishment or of coming to the Fire, unlike And on the day that the enemies of Allah shall be gathered (yuḥsharu, from ḥashr) to the Fire, then they shall be formed into groups. Until they come to it (41:19-20).

Its placement after the creature from the earth, a sign preceding the Resurrection, and before the Trumpet and the events of the Day of Resurrection, further indicates a gathering before the final Resurrection. The attempt to explain the reversed sequence as a way of separately emphasizing several catastrophes is contrived; if that were intended, the text should first have located this gathering after the Trumpet and then prevented the supposed misunderstanding. Thus the apparent sense is a pre-Resurrection gathering, though the wording is not so explicit that another interpretation is impossible.
verses.84: Al-Mizan explains that, when they arrive at the station where God addresses them, they will be rebuked for rejecting signs that point to the truth without having comprehensive knowledge of them. Their accusation that those signs were false and not binding proofs was therefore made without knowledge. The question, “Or what was it that you did?” rhetorically means that they did nothing but reject God’s signs; they had no other occupation that could excuse their turning away.
verses.85:
Al-Mizan reads bi-mā ẓalamū causally: the word falls upon them because of their injustice. Their silence follows from that divine word. The more plausible meaning is that, because they unjustly rejected God’s signs, they were not guided to anything that could exempt them from punishment, and so are cut off from speech.

The commentary allows that the word may mean the divine decree of punishment against the unjust, but considers this less fitting than the preceding explanation in the flow of the passage. It rejects interpreting the word as their actual punishment and entrance into the Fire, since that does not accord with the stated consequence, “so they shall not speak.”
verses.86:
Al-Mizan treats the verse as a further rebuke of those who deny God’s signs without knowledge. They can themselves observe the restful night and the illuminating day, through which they may see the signs in heaven and earth; their failure to open their eyes is therefore blameworthy.

The night’s suitability for rest and the day’s brightness for movement and sight are signs of God’s unity and of the religious teachings founded upon it, for receptive believers. They also teach that one should remain silent concerning what is obscured by the darkness of ignorance, neither speak without knowledge nor reject what one does not comprehend. Rather, one should proclaim and believe the clear signs that are manifest like the bright day.
verses.87:
Al-Mizan explains the blowing of the Trumpet metaphorically as a signal by which a multitude is collectively directed, like an army summoned to gather or march. Fazaʿ is the inward contraction and aversion caused by a frightening event, akin to anxiety, and dukhūr is abasement or dishonor.

Some interpreters take the verse as the second blast, which restores life for final judgment. The appearance of all before God, the exception for those God wills, and the later statement that some are secure from terror support this reading. Others take it as the first blast, at which living beings die, understanding their swooning as caused by terror and their coming to God as their return through death.

The commentary suggests that the Trumpet may be understood absolutely, as including both blasts: the first causes death and may concern the terror and the mountains’ movement, while the second gives life and may concern the universal coming before God in abasement. This accounts for the features appealed to by both interpretations. Those whom God wills are excluded from the universal terror, as clarified by: and they shall be secure from terror on the day (27:89).

Yet all beings, including those secure from terror, return to and appear before God. The exception of the purified servants (al-mukhlaṣūn) in: They shall most surely be brought up. But not the servants of Allah, the purified ones (37:127-128) means that they are exempted from reckoning and questioning, not from returning to God; the Resurrection encompasses every soul. Abasement before God does not diminish His friends’ honor, since a servant’s honor lies in abasement and poverty before Him. For His enemies, who falsely claimed honor, it is humiliating abasement.
verses.88:
Al-Mizan holds that the surrounding Resurrection context requires the mountains’ movement to be an event of that Day. The address depicts the scene to the Prophet: he will see mountains pass like clouds when the Trumpet is blown, though at present they are thought solid and motionless. The latter phrase may be parenthetical or describe the state of the one addressed.

Their apparent destruction is nevertheless the handiwork of God, Who has perfected everything. It is not disorder or the deprivation of beings from their perfection, but the bringing of every being to its appointed end, whether happiness or wretchedness. Thus the destruction of this world is the construction of the hereafter.

The commentary rejects the view that God’s awareness of deeds merely justifies the perfection of the Trumpet’s events as contrary to the context. It instead connects His awareness to the Day when the Trumpet is blown and all come before Him abased: He knows their deeds and requites them accordingly, rewarding those who bring good with better than it and casting those who bring evil into the Fire on their faces. This is why the following verses elaborate the meaning of His awareness; the shift in “Shall you be rewarded (for) aught except what you did?” intensifies the rebuke. The third-person recitation yafʿalūna, “what they do,” is preferred to the second-person reading.

Two other readings are considered. One takes the verse as trans-substantial motion (al-ḥarakat al-jawhariyyah), in which the substance of things is already moving toward its resurrection and return to God; this is especially pertinent to the phrase suggesting that mountains move while seeming solid. The other takes it as the earth’s translational motion. Although sound in isolation, that reading detaches the verse from its Resurrection context and leaves no connection between the mountains’ movement and “surely He is Aware of what you do.”
verses.89: Al-Mizan presents this verse, together with the next, as an elaboration of God’s awareness of human deeds through reward and punishment. Whoever brings good receives something better than the deed, because the deed is a means and preliminary, whereas its reward is the intended end, and the end is superior to its means. The terror from which such people are secure is, in context, the terror following the second blast of the Trumpet, as in: The great terror shall not grieve them, and the angels shall meet them: This is your day which you were promised (21:103).
verses.90:
Al-Mizan explains that the literal expression, “their faces will be thrown down,” metaphorically means that the evildoers themselves will be cast face-down into the Fire. The rhetorical question, “shall you be rewarded (for) aught except what you did?” negates any alternative: their recompense is their own deed made manifest and inseparable from them, so no injustice occurs in God’s judgment.

Verses 27:89-90 describe the respective recompenses of one who brings only good and one engulfed in evil. The position of one bearing both good and evil may be generally understood from these two cases, but its detailed account belongs elsewhere.
verses.91:
Al-Mizan explains that the final three verses conclude the chapter by defining the Prophet’s call as glad tidings and warning. It establishes the proof against people, but their affair belongs to God, who will show them His signs and is not heedless of their deeds.

The implied speaker is the Prophet: he is commanded to worship the Lord of Mecca, the sacred city. Calling God “the Lord of this city” and identifying it as sacred both honor Mecca and rebuke its people, who should have thanked God by worshipping Him alone rather than turning to idols. “His are all things” prevents the mistaken notion that He is merely Mecca’s Lord, like the polytheists’ alleged gods who each supposedly possessed only some part of the universe.

The Prophet is also commanded to be among those who submit to God’s will and decree. Such submission accords with the direction of human creation and fiṭrah; it is Abraham’s pure religion.
verses.92:
Al-Mizan explains that the Prophet is commanded not only to worship but to recite the Qur’an to the people. Whoever is guided through it benefits only his own soul; the Prophet gains nothing from another’s guidance. Whoever turns from his Lord’s remembrance and thereby goes astray bears his own unbelief and misguidance.

The Prophet’s task is warning, not guardianship over people; God is their guardian. The wording “then say: I am only one of the warners,” rather than simply “I am only one of the warners,” reminds him that their affairs are not entrusted to him. He must rely on his Lord and leave to God the case of those who stray.
verses.93:
Al-Mizan explains this concluding command as continuing the Prophet’s declaration that he is only a warner. Praise belongs to God for governing His kingdom: He calls people to what secures their good and felicity, guides those who believe in His signs and submit, and, with deniers, causes their hearts to die and their ears and eyes to be unresponsive, so that they stray and reject His communications.

God’s promised signs are understood generally as all signs that compel recognition of the truth, including those shown before and after the Hour. His not being heedless of people’s deeds explains His dealings with them: calling them to truth, guiding believers, leading deniers astray, displaying signs at the Resurrection, and recompensing good-doers and evildoers according to their deeds.

In “your Lord,” the singular pronoun addresses the Prophet, while “what you do” addresses all servants. The alternative third-person recitation yaʿmalūna, “what they do,” is perhaps preferable, for it gives the deniers a warning. Calling Him “your Lord” also consoles and strengthens the Prophet.
